places.name: Kenya
places.title: Kenya — Living systems, wildlife and ecological context | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore Kenya as a living system: forests, grasslands, drylands, wetlands, coastal and marine ecosystems, protected areas, pressures, sources and an ATLAS map.
places.summary: Kenya spans multiple ecological zones and habitats, including lowland and mountain forests, wooded and open grasslands, semi-arid scrubland, dry woodlands, inland aquatic systems, wetlands, and coastal and marine ecosystems.
places.truthBoundary: This page is a source-grounded country-scale discovery object. The ATLAS bounding box is a navigation extent, not an official administrative or ecological boundary. Protected-area totals and coverage figures use different source definitions and must not be collapsed.
places.protectedAreasSummary: Protected Planet's September 2026 country profile lists 374 protected areas. Kenya Wildlife Service separately states that its national parks, national reserves and national sanctuaries cover 8.2% of Kenya's land mass. These are different measures with different coverage and definitions.

sources.label: Kenya Wildlife Service — Protected Area Management
sources.use: Protected-area framework, conservation areas and KWS land-coverage statement.

sources.label: Kenya Wildlife Service — Ecosystems, Land and Seascapes Conservation
sources.use: KWS ecosystem-management scope including forests, wetlands, savannas and marine ecosystems.

sources.label: Convention on Biological Diversity — Kenya Country Profile
sources.use: Ecological-zone and habitat summary. CBD labels the profile text as draft; 4PLANET preserves that limitation.

sources.label: GBIF — Kenya
sources.use: Country-scale biodiversity occurrence-data entry point; occurrence records are not population estimates or complete range.

sources.label: Protected Planet — Kenya
sources.use: September 2026 protected-area profile and source inventory.

sources.label: Kenya Wildlife Service — Strategic Plan 2024–2028
sources.use: KWS-described pressures including habitat fragmentation, human–wildlife conflict, poaching and climate change.

places.name: Serengeti
places.title: Serengeti — Migration, savanna wildlife and ecological context | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore Serengeti as a connected savanna system: migration, water, predators, protected-area context, source evidence and ATLAS-linked species.
places.summary: Serengeti National Park sits at the heart of a wider East African ecosystem shaped by seasonal rainfall, grasslands, rivers, woodlands and one of the world's largest terrestrial migrations.
places.truthBoundary: This is a source-grounded discovery object centred on Serengeti National Park and its wider ecological context. The ATLAS rectangle is navigation geometry, not the UNESCO or national-park legal boundary. Wildlife counts quoted by UNESCO are source-reported site context, not current 4PLANET population estimates.
places.protectedAreasSummary: UNESCO describes the World Heritage property as 1,476,300 hectares and places it within a larger Serengeti ecosystem. Protected Planet separately records national and World Heritage designations with different reported areas; 4PLANET does not collapse those designations into one boundary or area figure.

sources.label: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Serengeti National Park
sources.use: Savanna, migration, biodiversity, integrity and management-pressure context; UNESCO's property boundary remains authoritative for the World Heritage site.

sources.label: Protected Planet — Serengeti National Park
sources.use: Current protected-area/World Heritage designation record and source provenance.

sources.label: GBIF — Tanzania
sources.use: Country-scale biodiversity-data entry point; GBIF records are observations, not population estimates or complete range.

places.name: Costa Rica
places.title: Costa Rica — Forests, wetlands, coasts and biodiversity | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore Costa Rica as a connected living system: forests, wetlands, mangroves, protected areas, biodiversity sources, Jaguar and ATLAS context.
places.summary: Costa Rica connects tropical forests, wetlands, high-elevation páramo, mangroves and marine-coastal systems through a national network of conservation areas and protected wildlife areas.
places.truthBoundary: This page is a country-scale discovery object, not a complete national biodiversity assessment. The CBD country profile used here is explicitly marked draft by the Secretariat. The ATLAS rectangle is navigation geometry, not an official national or ecological boundary dataset.
places.protectedAreasSummary: SINAC organises national conservation management through 11 Conservation Areas and publishes the country's protected-wildlife-area categories and records. 4PLANET preserves SINAC's management definitions rather than inventing a single protected-area coverage figure.
pressures: Connectivity between protected and productive landscapes

sources.label: SINAC — Conservation Areas
sources.use: Official national conservation-area structure.

sources.label: SINAC — Protected Wildlife Areas
sources.use: Official protected-wildlife-area categories and management context.

sources.label: Convention on Biological Diversity — Costa Rica Country Profile
sources.use: Country-scale ecosystem and biodiversity context. CBD labels this profile draft; that limitation is retained.

places.name: Great Barrier Reef
places.title: Great Barrier Reef — Coral, turtles, heat signals and evidence | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore the Great Barrier Reef through coral habitats, seagrass, mangroves, marine species, current reef-condition evidence and ATLAS context.
places.summary: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef ecosystem and includes coral reefs, seagrass beds, mangroves, islands, deep-water features and highly connected marine habitats.
places.truthBoundary: This page distinguishes the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area, Marine Park management context and monitoring evidence. The ATLAS rectangle is navigation geometry, not a statutory boundary. AIMS survey results describe surveyed reefs and regions, not every reef or the whole ecosystem at identical condition.
places.protectedAreasSummary: UNESCO records the World Heritage property at about 348,000 km². Reef Authority describes more than 2,900 coral reefs and 70 bioregions; these are different ecological/administrative descriptors and are kept separate.

sources.label: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority — Biodiversity
sources.use: Official Reef biodiversity, habitats and bioregion context.

sources.label: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority — Marine Turtles
sources.use: Green-turtle and marine-turtle occurrence, habitat and nesting context.

sources.label: AIMS — Annual Summary Report of Coral Reef Condition 2025/26
sources.use: Current 2025–26 surveyed-reef coral-cover and heat/bleaching context, with survey limitations.

sources.label: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Great Barrier Reef
sources.use: World Heritage property identity, extent and biodiversity context.

places.name: Norway
places.title: Norway — Coasts, forests, mountains and species observations | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore Norway through coastal and marine systems, forests, wetlands, mountains, public biodiversity data and ATLAS-linked species.
places.summary: Norway spans strong ecological gradients from southern forests and humid coasts to inland valleys, mountains and Arctic environments, with extensive marine systems connected to the mainland.
places.truthBoundary: This is a country-scale discovery object. The ATLAS rectangle covers mainland Norway and is navigation geometry, not a legal boundary; Svalbard has its own Place object and is not represented by this mainland map extent. Artskart observations are reported records from multiple data owners and do not prove complete range, abundance or current presence.
places.protectedAreasSummary: Norway uses the Natur i Norge (NiN) system to describe ecological variation. Artsdatabanken's Artskart aggregates species observations from multiple data owners and GBIF Norway; 4PLANET treats those as observations with source ownership and quality limits, not a complete national census.
pressures: Sampling and coverage gaps in biodiversity observations

sources.label: Convention on Biological Diversity — Norway Country Profile
sources.use: Country-scale ecological diversity and habitat-gradient context.

sources.label: Artsdatabanken — Artskart
sources.use: Norwegian species-observation discovery and provenance model; records originate from multiple data owners and GBIF Norway.

sources.label: Miljødirektoratet — Naturkart / Natur i Norge
sources.use: Official use of NiN for mapping and describing ecological variation in Norway.

places.name: Amazon Basin
places.title: Amazon Basin — Rainforest, rivers, Jaguar and ecological connectivity | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore the Amazon Basin through rainforest, freshwater connectivity, Jaguar, pressures, source evidence and 4PLANET ATLAS.
places.summary: The Amazon is the world's largest rainforest and river system, spanning multiple South American countries and connecting immense forest and freshwater networks.
places.truthBoundary: This is a transboundary basin-scale discovery object. The ATLAS rectangle is navigation geometry, not a legal basin, national or protected-area boundary. WWF figures are organisation-published regional context and must not be interpreted as a current 4PLANET census.
places.protectedAreasSummary: No single protected-area percentage is presented because the Amazon spans multiple countries, legal systems and protected-area categories. Protection, Indigenous territories and other land designations require their own authoritative boundary datasets.

sources.label: WWF — Amazon
sources.use: Basin/biome scale, forest/freshwater connectivity, biodiversity and pressure context.

sources.label: WWF — Protecting the Amazon's critical wildlife areas
sources.use: Jaguar and migratory freshwater-species connectivity research context; connectivity is not a complete distribution map.

sources.label: WWF — Amazon facts
sources.use: Independent public explainer within the same publisher family used only as a secondary cross-check on rainforest/river-system and threat context.

places.name: Congo Basin
places.title: Congo Basin — Forests, great apes, rivers and ecological context | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore the Congo Basin through tropical forest, freshwater systems, Chimpanzee, Eastern Gorilla, pressures, sources and ATLAS.
places.summary: The Congo Basin contains the world's second-largest tropical forest after the Amazon and a broad mosaic of rivers, dense forests, savannas, wetlands and tropical peatlands across Central Africa.
places.truthBoundary: This is a transboundary ecological discovery object, not one legal or protected-area boundary. Great-ape species and subspecies occupy different parts of the basin; a basin-level link does not imply uniform distribution or population condition.
places.protectedAreasSummary: No single protected-area total is presented for the basin. Protected areas, community lands and national management systems differ across six countries and must retain their own legal/source identities.
pressures: Mining, fossil-fuel extraction and infrastructure fragmentation

sources.label: WWF — Congo Basin
sources.use: Basin-scale forest/freshwater mosaic, biodiversity, great-ape and pressure context.

sources.label: WWF — Gorilla habituation in the Congo Basin
sources.use: Current 2026 example of gorilla monitoring/conservation in northern Congo Basin; not transferable to all gorilla populations.

sources.label: WWF — Chimpanzee
sources.use: Species habitat and pressure context for one curated species connection; does not establish basin-wide occupancy.

places.name: Borneo
places.title: Borneo — Rainforest, Orangutan and forest connectivity | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore Borneo through tropical forest, Bornean Orangutan, habitat fragmentation, source evidence and 4PLANET ATLAS.
places.summary: Borneo is a major Southeast Asian tropical-forest island shared by Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei, with globally important rainforest and peatland biodiversity.
places.truthBoundary: This is an island-scale ecological discovery object, not a national or protected-area boundary. Bornean Orangutan subspecies, population estimates and habitat conditions vary across the island and must remain source-specific.
places.protectedAreasSummary: No single protected-area percentage is shown because Borneo spans three national jurisdictions and multiple land/protection categories. Forest cover, concessions and protected-area boundaries require source-specific spatial layers.

sources.label: WWF — Borneo and Sumatra
sources.use: Regional forest, deforestation, commodity and wildlife-pressure context.

sources.label: WWF — Bornean Orangutan
sources.use: Bornean Orangutan habitat, subspecies and pressure context; population figures remain source-published estimates.

sources.label: WWF — Where orangutans live
sources.use: Secondary cross-check for Borneo/Sumatra rainforest dependence and broad pressure context.

places.name: Svalbard
places.title: Svalbard — Sea ice, Polar Bear, whales and protected Arctic nature | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore Svalbard through sea ice, marine and terrestrial ecosystems, Polar Bear, whales, protected areas, sources and ATLAS.
places.summary: Svalbard links Arctic land, fjords, sea ice and marine food webs. Energy moves strongly between sea and land through seabirds, marine mammals and other species adapted to polar conditions.
places.truthBoundary: This is a Svalbard-scale discovery object. The ATLAS rectangle is navigation geometry, not the statutory boundary of the Svalbard archipelago or any protected area. Population and sea-ice conditions vary through time and by subpopulation/site.
places.protectedAreasSummary: The Governor of Svalbard reported on 23 September 2026 that Svalbard has seven national parks, 21 nature reserves and one geotopic conservation area, covering about 65% of land and 84% of territorial waters. These are Governor-reported legal protection figures, not ecological-condition scores.

sources.label: Norwegian Polar Institute — Fauna in Svalbard
sources.use: Sea–land ecosystem linkage, marine mammals, whales, Polar Bear, ice-fauna and climate-pressure context.

sources.label: Norwegian Polar Institute — Polar Bear
sources.use: Polar Bear distribution, Svalbard/Barents Sea population context, sea-ice dependence and explicit uncertainty.

sources.label: Governor of Svalbard — Protected areas in Svalbard
sources.use: Current 23 Sep 2026 legal protected-area counts and reported land/water coverage.

places.name: Oslofjord
places.title: Oslofjord — Cod, Blue Mussel, pollution and restoration evidence | 4PLANET
places.description: Explore Oslofjord through marine ecological condition, Cod, Blue Mussel, pollution evidence, fisheries measures, sources and ATLAS.
places.summary: Oslofjord is a heavily used fjord system where wastewater, agricultural runoff, fisheries and other human pressures interact with marine habitats, food webs and coastal communities.
places.truthBoundary: This is a fjord-scale discovery object, not a complete condition assessment. Official ecological/chemical classifications, monitoring samples, fishing rules and restoration areas measure different things and remain separate. The ATLAS rectangle is navigation geometry, not a statutory fjord boundary.
places.protectedAreasSummary: 4PLANET does not collapse marine national parks, three 2026 no-fishing areas, restoration sites and water-management classifications into one protected-area metric. Each has different legal purpose and spatial definition.
pressures: Fishing pressure and depleted coastal fish populations

sources.label: Norwegian Government — Oslofjorden
sources.use: Current government summary of serious ecosystem condition, main pressures and 2026 policy/restoration context.

sources.label: Norwegian Environment Agency — coastal contaminant monitoring 2024
sources.use: Annual monitoring evidence; Oslofjord sediment exceedances and explicit difficulty obtaining enough Cod samples.

sources.label: Norwegian Environment Agency — contaminants in Oslofjord food webs
sources.use: 2025 Urban Fjord sampling across sediment and food-web organisms including Blue Mussel and Cod; sampled evidence is not whole-fjord condition.
